sentences.text: There are wolves in that part of the Abruzzo — properly, verifiably, in numbers, since the protections came in — and everybody in both villages knows it and nobody makes a fuss.
The one on the ridge is different only in that she is regular.
She walks the old mule track.

Not near it, not roughly along it: on it, the full length, from the last house at Colle to the last house at Fonte, most nights between October and March, and she has been doing it for something over eleven years.
There is nothing remarkable in a wolf using a track.
It is the least remarkable thing about her.

A wolf on the move will take the easiest line through cover exactly the way anything does, and a mule track cut into a hillside in the Roman period is, by construction, the easiest line over that ridge, and it does not stop being the easiest line because two comuni stopped speaking in 1974.
She is not walking between the villages.
She is walking over the ridge, and the villages happen to be at the two ends of the only sensible way over it, which is why they are where they are.
Both villages know.
Both villages have known for a decade.

There are camera-trap photographs of her in the bar at Colle and there are camera-trap photographs of her in the bar at Fonte and they are, as far as Dario can establish, the same photographs, because they came off the same trap.
The trap belongs to the national park.

It is on a beech about halfway up on the Colle side, in a place that is technically in the comune of Colle by about sixty metres, and the park sends the images to both village halls because the park does not have a position on 1974 and has never been asked to develop one.
That is the joke, and both villages make it, separately, in exactly the same words, and neither of them knows the other one makes it.
Dario found the mule track at eleven because he was following her tracks in snow and did not think about where he was going until he came out at the top and saw the roofs of Fonte below him.
He stood there for a long time.
He was closer to Fonte than to his own house.
He had never in his life seen it from above.
It is a completely ordinary Abruzzese village.
Twenty-odd roofs, a bell tower, a road going down, a football pitch with one net.
He had spent eleven years understanding Fonte as a word people did not say at his grandfather's table and it turned out to be twenty-odd roofs.
